Famous philosophy quotes

A gallery of widely recognized passages — lines that have been read, taught, and argued with for centuries. Each one links to a full archive entry that names the work, the passage, and the edition it comes from.

Famous and well-sourced are different properties. A line can be famous because it circulates, and a famous line can be a compression of something the philosopher actually wrote. The archive entries behind these passages record both: where the words sit, and what forms circulate in their place.

What makes a philosophy quote famous

Not brevity, and not comfort. The passages on this page survived because they carry an argument in a form that sticks: Socrates refusing exile rather than stop examining lives, Marcus Aurelius telling himself to get out of bed, Descartes locating his own existence inside the one doubt he could not shake. Fame in philosophy is usually the fame of a position a reader can still take sides on.

It also makes them the most misquoted sentences in the language. “I know that I know nothing” is a later compression of a more careful claim; “knowledge is power” drops the clause that made Bacon's aphorism an argument. If you plan to quote one of these lines in print, the archive entry — not this gallery — is the thing to cite, because only the entry carries the locator and the attribution notes.

Suspect a famous line's attribution? Trace it to its source or check the misattributed register.
